title: Melting ice in Norway's highest mountains reveals 6,000-year-old arrows and toys
dek: Archaeologists are recovering prehistoric arrows, clothing, and children's toys from ice that has remained frozen for millennia. The finds are rewriting textbooks on Stone Age mountain use.
body: At 2,000 metres above sea level in Norway's highest mountains, archaeologists from the Secrets of the Ice programme recovered 48 prehistoric arrows during the latest field season. The oldest examples date to between 5,000 and 6,000 years ago, far older than the Viking Age and medieval artefacts that dominated earlier ice finds.

The discoveries are challenging previous interpretations of how Norway's mountainous landscapes were used during the Stone and Bronze Ages. According to archaeologist Julian Robert Post-Melbye of the University of Oslo, textbooks on the prehistory of the Norwegian mountains will have to be rewritten.

Researchers are finding more than hunting equipment. Clothing, tools, everyday objects, and even children's toys are emerging along ancient mountain routes. Post-Melbye said it turns out that high in the mountains, not only hunters but also farmers, craftsmen, travellers, and even children were present.

Many finds are connected with prehistoric reindeer hunting. During warmer summer conditions, reindeer travelled from valleys onto patches of snow and ice to escape insects and regulate their body temperature. Stone Age hunters appear to have understood this behaviour and positioned themselves where the animals congregated.

Archaeologists frequently recover arrows and arrowheads from these hunting grounds, including projectiles that missed their targets and became embedded in snow before eventually being incorporated into the ice. The presence of artefacts dating back several thousand years does not indicate these areas were ice-free when prehistoric hunters visited them.

Instead, the finds demonstrate that ancient people were actively using the surface of ice patches that have remained largely undisturbed for millennia. The ice has created exceptional preservation conditions for materials that would normally decay rapidly. Organic remains including wood, leather, bone, textiles, and feathers can survive for thousands of years when permanently frozen.

Once exposed to air and changing temperatures, however, deterioration can begin almost immediately. Modern archaeological practice generally aims to leave portions of sites undisturbed for future generations. At melting ice sites, researchers may have only a short period to identify and recover newly exposed objects. Post-Melbye said at 2,000 metres they have only days, maybe weeks, to secure the finds.

At some locations Post-Melbye has studied during the past 15 years, around half of the ice has already disappeared. Researchers estimate that many ice patches containing archaeological material could vanish completely within the next two decades. The discoveries have also raised the possibility that Norwegian ice could eventually reveal preserved human remains comparable to Ötzi, the approximately 5,000-year-old natural mummy discovered in the Ötztal Alps in 1991.
doesnt_show: The finds do not show that the mountain areas were ice-free during the Stone Age; rather, people used the surface of persistent ice patches. The possibility of finding human remains like Ötzi remains speculative and would require an exceptional sequence of preservation events.
settle: Systematic survey of all remaining ice patches before they vanish, combined with radiocarbon dating of newly exposed organic material, would clarify the full chronological range and nature of high-elevation use.
